package.name: Time
package.description: Durations, monotonic clocks and wall clocks

modules.name: Calendar
modules.header:
The proleptic Gregorian calendar, extended backwards as if it had always been in force.
A date is a year, a month and a day that actually exists: February 29th only in a leap year, the 31st only in
the months that have one. The conversion to and from a flat day count is the civil-calendar arithmetic that
treats March as the first month, which puts the leap day last and turns the month lengths into one formula --
the standard trick, worth having exactly once.
Leap seconds are deliberately absent from `TimeOfDay`: a second is 0 to 59, and what to do about 23:59:60 is a
parsing policy decided where text comes in, not a representation question.

modules.name: CalendarArithmetic
modules.header:
Moving through the calendar, with the awkward cases decided rather than discovered.
Days are the honest unit: adding days is adding to the epoch count, total and exact. Months and years are not --
the 31st of January has no counterpart one month on, and the leap day none one year on — so those operations
need a policy, and the policy here is **clamp to the month's end**: January 31st plus a month is the last day of
February, and February 29th plus a year is February 28th. Clamping is what a human means by "same day next
month" when the day is missing, and it keeps the operation total; the alternative, refusing, would make month
arithmetic fail on a third of the calendar.
What is deliberately deferred: IANA time zones and discovering the machine's local zone. Both are a database
with a release cycle, not arithmetic, and pretending otherwise is how software is wrong twice a year.

modules.name: CalendarParse
modules.header:
Reading a calendar value out of text, and saying exactly what was wrong with it.
The old parser answered `bool` and wrote through output slots, which made every failure the same failure. A
caller could not tell a typo from a February the thirtieth, and could not point at the character: both are
"false", and both leave the caller re-reading its own input to guess.
So every parser here answers a `Result` and every failure carries a zero-based byte offset into the text it was
given. The categories are the ones a caller acts on differently. A malformed shape is the writer's mistake and
the offset is where the shape stopped matching. An invalid month, a nonexistent day and an out-of-range time are
well-formed text naming something that does not exist, which is a different mistake and usually a different
bug. An excessive fraction and an out-of-range offset are each a field that parsed and then would not fit.
End of input is an offset like any other: it is the text's length, which is where the missing character would
have gone.
The four entry points share their machinery rather than reimplementing it, so `ParseRfc3339` cannot disagree
with `ParseDate` about what a date is.

modules.name: CalendarText
modules.header:
What a calendar value looks like, and what it refuses to pretend to know.
The whole design here is one decision applied four times: a value renders what it holds and never invents what it
does not. A `DateTime` is a date and a time with no offset field, so it renders without one — not with `Z`, which
would claim UTC, and not with the machine's local offset, which would claim a place. A reader who wants an offset
in the text attaches one and renders an `OffsetDateTime`, which has somewhere to keep it.
That is why `OffsetDateTime` exists at all. RFC 3339 requires an offset, so a type that cannot carry one cannot
produce RFC 3339, and the alternative — letting `DateTime` take an offset argument at render time — puts the
decision in the wrong place: a format call has no way to pass one.
The renderers write digits directly rather than borrowing Format's integer machinery, which they could not do
anyway without Time depending on it. Every field here has a known width, so the loops are fixed and nothing
allocates: a year is four digits or as many as it needs, everything else is exactly two.

modules.name: Duration
modules.header:
A span of time, exact to the nanosecond.
A duration is seconds plus a nanosecond fraction, and the fraction is always in [0, 1e9): the value is
`seconds + nanoseconds / 1e9` with the sign carried entirely by the seconds. That single invariant is what makes
equality bytewise, ordering two comparisons, and arithmetic a carry — minus one and a half seconds is seconds
-2 and half a billion nanoseconds, not two fields that each carry a sign and can disagree.
The arithmetic is checked. A duration overflows at about 292 billion years, which no honest computation reaches,
so an overflow is a bug in the caller's arithmetic — and the answer to a bug is a report, not a wrap that turns
a timeout into a deadline in the past.

modules.name: DurationText
modules.header:
A span of time as text, and back.
The form is signed decimal seconds with an `s`: `1.5s`, `-0.25s`, `0s`. One unit rather than a broken-down
`1h30m` because a duration is a number, and a number with one unit compares, sorts and round-trips without a
grammar. `seconds` names the same form explicitly, for a caller who wants the intent in the placeholder.
The negative case is the one worth care. A `Duration` is normalized as `seconds + nanoseconds / 1e9` with the
fraction always in [0, 1e9), so minus one and a half seconds is *not* seconds = -1 and nanoseconds = 5e8: it is
seconds = -2 and nanoseconds = 5e8, because -2 + 0.5 is -1.5. Rendering the fields as they sit would produce
"-2.5s", which is wrong by two seconds and looks plausible. The magnitude has to be recomputed, and it is
computed in `uint64` so that the most negative duration — whose magnitude has no positive counterpart in
`int64` — comes out right rather than wrapping to itself.

modules.name: Instant
modules.header:
A point on the clock that only moves forward.
The monotonic clock answers one question — how much time passed between two readings — and answers it even
while somebody sets the wall clock, which is exactly when the wall clock answers it wrongly. An `Instant` means
nothing as a number: it has no epoch, no calendar, and no meaning in another process. What it has is that a
later reading minus an earlier one is the time that really elapsed.
Sleeping used to live here, because it is the same clock's other direction. It moved to `Sleep.rux` when it
grew a failure to report and a chunking loop to drive, which is more than a clock reading needs next to it.

modules.name: InstantText
modules.header:
What a monotonic reading looks like to somebody inspecting a program, and why it has no reader's form.
`Instant` implements `Debug` and deliberately does not implement `Display`. The absence is the design, not an
omission waiting to be filled in. `Display` is the text a value has for a reader, and a reading of the monotonic
clock has none: it is a count from an origin the system chose at boot, it means nothing in another process, and
it names no moment anybody can look up. A reader handed "812349871234" learns nothing true. What is meaningful is
the difference between two readings, and that difference is a `Duration`, which renders itself.
So the only rendering here is the diagnostic one. It shows the tick count, because that is the only thing the
value holds, and it wraps it in the type's name and the unit so that nobody reads it as a moment: `Instant(...)`
is visibly a reading of something rather than a time, and `nanoseconds:` says what the number counts. Debug
output is diagnostic and promises no round trip, which is exactly the right promise for a number whose meaning
ends with the process that produced it.

modules.name: Sleep
modules.header:
Waiting for a whole span, and saying so when the wait did not happen.
Sleeping looks like the simplest thing in this package and has three ways to be quietly wrong, all of which this
module used to have.
A signal can cut a Unix wait short. The loop goes back for the remainder rather than returning early, because a
caller asked for a span, not for a span unless the process happened to receive a signal.
Windows takes its interval as a 32-bit millisecond count, which runs out after about 49.7 days. Clamping a longer
span to that ceiling is what the previous version did, and it returned as though it had slept for the whole
hundred days it was asked for. A span longer than the ceiling is now waited for in chunks.
And a wait can simply fail. `nanosleep` reports `EINVAL` for a request it will not honor, and the previous
version could not tell that from a completed sleep — both left the remainder at zero — so it returned success
having waited for nothing at all. The wait now reports a `TimeError`, and a caller that ignores it is at least
making that choice.
The system wait is reached through the `Waiter` interface so that the chunking and the retry loop can be tested
against an injected one. A test for a hundred-day sleep must not take a hundred days, and a test for an
interrupted sleep cannot arrange a signal.

modules.name: Timestamp
modules.header:
The wall clock, in UTC, as a count from the Unix epoch.
A timestamp is what the machine believes the time is: it jumps when the clock is set, drifts until NTP pulls it
back, and two machines disagree about it. That is not a defect to paper over — it is what a wall clock is, and
the reason `Instant` exists for measuring. What a timestamp is for is naming a moment so another machine, or a
later run, can recognize it.
The representation is seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00 UTC and a nanosecond fraction, normalized exactly as a
`Duration` is: fraction in [0, 1e9), sign in the seconds, so a moment before the epoch is negative seconds and a
fraction counting up. Windows counts from 1601 in hundred-nanosecond ticks, and the conversion is one constant
the platform package already carries.

modules.name: TimestampText
modules.header:
The wall clock as text, in one form unless the caller says otherwise.
A timestamp is two things at once — a moment on the calendar and a count of seconds — and a type that renders
whichever one the caller seems to want is a type nobody can predict. So there is one default and it is the
calendar form: RFC 3339 in UTC, which is what a timestamp is for. Naming a moment so another machine recognizes
it is the reason the value exists, and 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z reads as a date to every reader and every parser
there is, where 0 reads as a date to neither.
The second count is still available and still exact, but it has to be asked for by name: `{:unix}`. That is the
whole of the "one default" rule. A style that selects between two renderings is a choice made at the placeholder,
where it is visible; a value that guesses is a choice made nowhere.
The calendar form has a range and the second count does not, which is the one place this file can fail on a value
rather than on a request. The package spells four-digit years — `Date::PlusDays` already treats that as the honest
bound, and RFC 3339 requires exactly four digits — so a moment outside years 0000 through 9999 has no RFC 3339
text at all. It is refused with `ValueOutOfRange` before anything is written, because a destination that has
already received "+2724" and then learns the value cannot be spelled is a destination holding a lie.

cases.name: InvalidSyntax
cases.doc:
The text does not have the shape required: a missing separator, a non-digit where a digit belongs, text
after the value, or input that stops early. The offset is where the shape stopped matching, which is the
text's length when it ran out.

cases.name: InvalidMonth
cases.doc: A well-formed two-digit month naming no month. The offset is the first of its digits.

cases.name: NonexistentDay
cases.doc:
A well-formed day that the month does not have, such as the thirtieth of February. The offset is the first
of its digits.

cases.name: InvalidTime
cases.doc:
A well-formed hour, minute or second outside its range. The offset is the first digit of the offending
field. Second 60 is not here: it is the leap second, and it folds rather than failing.

cases.name: ExcessiveFraction
cases.doc: More fraction digits than a nanosecond can hold. The offset is the first digit that could not be kept.

cases.name: InvalidOffset
cases.doc: A well-formed offset outside what an offset may be. The offset is the sign that opened it.

doc.summary: Reads `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fraction]`, with no offset.
doc.markdown:
Reads `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fraction]`, with no offset.
The separator may be `T`, `t` or a space, which is as far as the RFC 3339 liberality goes. No offset is read,
and one present is text after the value: a `DateTime` has nowhere to keep an offset, so accepting one would
discard it silently. `ParseRfc3339` is what reads a moment that carries one.
The failures `ParseDate` and `ParseTimeOfDay` report, at their offsets within this text.
doc.returns: the local date and time, or why the text is not one

items.name: ParseRfc3339
items.signature: pub func ParseRfc3339(text: char8[..]) -> OffsetDateTime ! TimeParseError

doc.summary: Reads `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fraction](Z|+HH:MM|-HH:MM)`.
doc.markdown:
Reads `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fraction](Z|+HH:MM|-HH:MM)`.
The offset is required, which is what RFC 3339 requires and what makes the result a moment rather than a local
reading. Second 60 folds to the last nanosecond of second 59, as this package's leap-second policy states;
formatting never produces second 60, so the fold is one-way and the round trip is clean for every ordinary
moment.
The failures the date, time and offset readers report, plus `InvalidSyntax` for text after the offset. Each
carries the byte offset where it was found.
doc.returns: the moment with the offset it was stated in, or why the text is not one

doc.summary: A date and time together with the offset from UTC they are stated in.
doc.markdown:

doc.summary: Why a wait did not happen.
doc.markdown:
Why a wait did not happen. `Copy`.
Every case is a failure. An interruption is not one: a waiter that was cut short succeeds with the part of the span
still to wait, and `SleepFor` goes back for it, because a caller that asked for a span asked for the whole span.

cases.name: InvalidDuration
cases.doc: The system refused the request itself, rather than being unable to finish it.

cases.name: Failed
cases.doc: The system reported a failure this module has no name for.

doc.summary: The longest interval one system wait may be asked for, in milliseconds.
doc.markdown:
The longest interval one system wait may be asked for, in milliseconds.
Windows takes a 32-bit count and reserves `0xFFFFFFFF` to mean "wait forever", so the largest finite request is
one less. Every system's wait is chunked to this so that the loop is the same everywhere and so that a test of
the chunking is a test of what actually runs.
About 49.7 days. A span longer than this is waited for in more than one chunk.

doc.summary: How long the next single wait should be asked for, given how much of the span is left.
doc.markdown:
How long the next single wait should be asked for, given how much of the span is left.
Returns the whole millisecond count to ask the system for: the remaining span rounded **up**, since a wait
promises at least what was asked and never less, or `MaximumWaitMilliseconds` when the remainder is longer than
one wait can express. Never zero for a positive span, so a loop driven by this always makes progress.
A negative or zero span gives zero, which is the value a caller uses to stop.
This is where the old clamp was, and it is public so that the hundred-day case can be checked without waiting a
hundred days.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: span
params.markdown: how much of the wait is left

doc.returns: the milliseconds to ask the system for

doc.summary: One wait, however the caller reaches the system.
doc.markdown:
One wait, however the caller reaches the system.
An implementation waits for at most `span` and reports what is left of it. Reporting less than the whole span as
remaining is how a wait says it did some of the work, including when a signal stopped it early; failing is how it
says the system refused. `SleepFor` drives whichever implementation it is given until nothing is left.

doc.markdown:
How many waits `SleepFor` will make before giving up on a span that never shrinks.

items.name: SleepUsing
items.signature: pub func SleepUsing<W: Waiter>(waiter: &var W, span: Duration) -> ! TimeError

doc.summary: Waits out `span` through `waiter`, retrying interruptions and chunking what one wait cannot express.
doc.markdown:
Waits out `span` through `waiter`, retrying interruptions and chunking what one wait cannot express.
A negative or zero span returns at once, having waited for nothing. Otherwise this calls `waiter` until it
reports that nothing is left, so an interruption is invisible to the caller and a span longer than one wait
takes several.
Fails with whatever the waiter failed with, having stopped there rather than asking again. Fails with `Failed`
when the waiter neither advanced nor failed `MaximumWaitAttempts` times running, which no real wait does and which
is what keeps a broken implementation from hanging a program.
doc.returns: nothing when the whole span was waited out, or why it was not

doc.summary: Stops the calling thread for at least `span`.
doc.markdown:
Stops the calling thread for at least `span`.
At least: the system wakes the thread no earlier, and how much later is the scheduler's business. A negative or
zero span returns at once.
A signal can interrupt the wait on the Unix systems, and this goes back for the remainder until the whole span
has passed — the interruption is invisible, which is what makes this safe to use for pacing. A span longer than
one system wait can express is waited for in chunks rather than clamped, so a hundred-day sleep is a hundred
days.
Fails with `InvalidDuration` when the system refused the request, which a normalized non-negative span should not
produce, and `Failed` for anything else. A caller with nothing to do about a failed wait says so with
`SleepFor(span) catch { else => {} }`; the point is that it is no longer indistinguishable from success.
doc.returns: nothing when the whole span was waited out, or why it was not

doc.summary: Whether this moment falls inside the years the calendar spells, and so has an RFC 3339 text.
doc.markdown:
Whether this moment falls inside the years the calendar spells, and so has an RFC 3339 text.
The bound is years 0000 through 9999, which is the range `Date` arithmetic already treats as the package's
own and the range RFC 3339's four year digits allow. A caller that must not meet a formatting failure asks
here first; one that renders through a placeholder learns the same thing as `ValueOutOfRange`.
Borrows the moment and leaves it untouched. Cannot fail; runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

members.signature: pub func WriteDisplay(self: &Timestamp, writer: &var TextWriter, spec: FormatSpec) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes the moment as RFC 3339 in UTC, or as the Unix second count under the `unix` style.
doc.markdown:
Writes the moment as RFC 3339 in UTC, or as the Unix second count under the `unix` style.
The calendar form is the default and the only one an unadorned placeholder produces: `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`
rather than `0`. `rfc3339` and `iso8601` name that same form explicitly, and `unix` asks for the signed
second count instead — a value with two readings does not get to guess which one a caller meant.
A precision names exactly that many fractional digits, 0 through 9, and truncates, in either form. Without
one the fraction is written to the digits it has with trailing zeros trimmed, and omitted when it is zero.
Reports whatever the writer reported, `UnsupportedRequest` for a style other than the three named above or
for a precision past nine, and `ValueOutOfRange` for a moment outside years 0000 through 9999, which RFC
3339's four year digits cannot spell. The range is checked before anything is written, so a refused moment
leaves the destination as it was.
doc.returns: success when the whole moment was accepted
